20 HP VFD Screw Air Compressor | 16 Bar | 60 CFM | Complete Air Treatment System for Laser Cutting & Fabrication

Reliable, stable, and properly treated compressed air is essential for fabrication industries where laser cutting machinery, CNC equipment, pneumatic tools, automation systems, and other production equipment require consistent air pressure. Sarv Jagat Corporation presents this complete 20 HP VFD Screw Air Compressor system, designed for high-pressure industrial applications and demanding fabrication requirements.

This complete setup features a 20 HP VFD Screw Air Compressor with Innovance Variable Frequency Drive technology, delivering approximately 60 CFM air capacity at a maximum working pressure of 16 bar. The system is integrated with a 500-litre air receiver tank, a 92–100 CFM refrigerated air dryer, a carbon tower, a pre-filter, an after-filter, a micro-filter, and a water separator.

The tank-mounted configuration provides a compact and organized compressed air solution by combining air generation, storage, moisture removal, and multi-stage filtration into one complete industrial setup.

Complete System Configuration

* 20 HP VFD Screw Air Compressor
* Inversion Variable Frequency Drive
* Maximum Working Pressure – 16 Bar
* Air Delivery – Approximately 60 CFM
* 500-Litre Air Receiver Tank
* 92–100 CFM Refrigerated Air Dryer
* Carbon Tower
* Pre-Filter
* After-Filter
* Micro Filter
* Water Separator
* Tank-Mounted Assembly
* Complete Compressed Air Treatment System

VFD Technology for Efficient Operation

The Innovance VFD helps adjust the compressor motor speed according to changing compressed air demand. Instead of operating continuously at a fixed speed, the compressor can respond to variations in air consumption.

This helps maintain stable system pressure and can improve energy efficiency during varying production loads. Smooth starting and automatic operation also support reliable performance in industrial environments.

For fabrication and laser cutting applications, selecting the correct compressor capacity, pressure, storage, and air-treatment equipment is important for maintaining dependable operation of downstream machinery.

Complete Air Storage and Treatment System

The 500-litre air receiver tank stores compressed air and helps stabilise pressure during changing air demand. It also provides an air reserve for connected equipment.

The water separator helps remove condensed moisture from the compressed air system. After this stage, the 92–100 CFM refrigerated air dryer helps reduce moisture content before the air reaches downstream machinery.

The pre-filter, after-filter, and micro-filter provide progressive air treatment to help reduce particles, oil aerosols, and other contaminants. The Carbon Tower provides an additional stage of air treatment for applications requiring improved compressed air quality.

Together, the compressor, receiver tank, dryer, separator, and filtration system form a complete compressed air package designed for demanding industrial operations.

title: Screw Air Compressor
excerpt: Screw compressors are rotary positive-displacement air compressors designed to provide a continuous and reliable supply of compressed air for industrial applications. Sarv Jagat offers screw compressor solutions in fixed-speed and VFD configurations for different pressure, airflow, and operating requirements.
content:
A screw compressor is a rotary positive-displacement compressor that uses two intermeshing screw rotors to compress air continuously. Compared with conventional reciprocating compressors, screw compressors are widely used where industries require a steady compressed-air supply, continuous operation, compact installation, and reliable performance.

Sarv Jagat screw compressors are available in fixed-speed and Variable Frequency Drive (VFD/VSD) configurations, with different motor capacities, pressure ratings, and Free Air Delivery (FAD) options to suit industrial requirements.

Typical applications include manufacturing plants, textile industries, automotive workshops, CNC and VMC machines, packaging, pharmaceuticals, food processing, engineering, fabrication, printing, plastics, and general industrial production.

A properly selected screw compressor should be matched to the actual air demand, working pressure, duty cycle, operating environment, and required air quality. Compressor sizing based only on motor HP can result in inefficient operation or inadequate air supply.

Sarv Jagat also provides complete compressed-air solutions including refrigerated air dryers, air receiver tanks, filters, moisture separators, automatic drain systems, and other air-treatment equipment, allowing industries to develop an integrated compressed-air system.

title: Complete Compressed Air Filtration System | Pre Filter, Dryer, After Filter & Carbon Filter
excerpt: Complete compressed air treatment system with pre-filter, refrigerated air dryer, after-filter, activated carbon filter, moisture separator, and automatic drain for cleaner and drier compressed air.
content:
Clean, dry, and properly treated compressed air is essential for reliable industrial operations. Sarv Jagat Corporation presents a complete compressed air treatment setup designed to improve air quality by reducing moisture, water, oil particles, oil vapour, and other contaminants from the compressed air system.

This general air treatment setup includes a pre-filter installed before the refrigerated air dryer, followed by an after-filter and activated carbon filter after the dryer. An air-water moisture separator with an automatic drain can also be installed after the air compressor or at the end of the compressed air system, depending on the application and system requirements. This complete arrangement helps deliver cleaner and drier compressed air for pneumatic machinery, automation systems, production equipment, and various industrial applications. ⚙️ Complete Air Treatment Setup ✅ Pre-filter before the refrigerated air dryer ✅ Refrigerated Air Dryer for Moisture Removal ✅ After-filter after the air dryer ✅ Activated Carbon Filter for Oil Vapour and Odour Reduction ✅ Air-Water/Moisture Separator ✅ Automatic Condensate Drain System ✅ Industrial Piping and Accessories ✅ Suitable for Complete Compressed Air Systems 🔧 How the System Works The pre-filter is installed before the refrigerated air dryer to help remove larger particles, water droplets, and other contaminants from the compressed air. The refrigerated air dryer then reduces moisture by cooling the compressed air and separating the condensed water. After the dryer, the after filter provides additional filtration for finer particles and contaminants. The activated carbon filter is used where further reduction of oil vapour and odour is required to improve the quality of compressed air supplied to downstream equipment and processes. The air-water moisture separator helps separate liquid water and moisture from the compressed air line. Its Automatic Drain system removes the collected condensate automatically, reducing the need for frequent manual draining. 🏭 Suitable Applications This compressed air filtration and treatment setup is suitable for: • Manufacturing Industries • Fabrication Units • CNC and Engineering Machines • Food Processing Machinery • Textile Machinery • Packaging Machines • Pharmaceutical Applications • Laser and Plasma Cutting • Automobile Industries • Plastic and Injection Moulding • Pneumatic Automation • General Industrial Machinery 🎥 This setup showcases how different compressed air treatment components can be arranged within an industrial compressed air system, including the pre-filter, refrigerated air dryer, after-filter, activated carbon filter, air-water separator, automatic drain, industrial piping, and other accessories. title: Quick Learning | Air Compressor Intake Filter | Cleaning, Maintenance & Efficiency
excerpt: Learn why a clean air intake filter is important for maintaining proper airflow, compressor efficiency, reliable operation, and long-term performance in industrial air compressor systems.
content:
A clean air intake filter is an important part of regular air compressor maintenance. During operation, the compressor continuously draws atmospheric air, and the intake filter helps prevent dust, dirt, and airborne particles from entering the compressor system.


When the intake filter becomes dirty or clogged, airflow can be restricted, and the compressor may need to work harder to maintain the required air supply. Regular inspection, cleaning, and timely replacement can help support efficient compressor operation and reduce unnecessary operating stress.


🔧 Dirty Air Filter vs Clean Air Filter

➜ Dirty or clogged filter → Restricted airflow
➜ Restricted airflow → Increased compressor load
➜ Increased load → Higher energy consumption
➜ Dust accumulation → Increased wear and tear
➜ Poor maintenance → Reduced compressor efficiency
➜ Long-term neglect → Potentially shorter equipment life

➜ Clean filter → Better airflow
➜ Proper air intake → Efficient compressor operation
➜ Regular cleaning → Reliable performance
➜ Proper maintenance → Supports longer equipment life


💡 Why Air Intake Filter Cleaning Is Important

Regular air filter inspection and cleaning help maintain adequate airflow into the compressor. This is particularly important for compressors operating in dusty or demanding environments such as manufacturing, fabrication, engineering, construction, textile, food processing, automotive, and other industrial applications.


Following the manufacturer's recommended cleaning and replacement schedule can help maintain compressor efficiency and support reliable long-term operation.


⚙️ Quick Maintenance Tips

➜ Inspect the air intake filter regularly.
➜ Clean the filter according to the manufacturer's recommendations.
➜ Check for excessive dust, dirt, or blockage.
➜ Replace the filter if it is damaged or cannot be cleaned properly.
➜ Maintain the complete compressor air intake system regularly.


🏭 Benefits of Proper Air Filter Maintenance

➜ Smooth compressor airflow
➜ Better energy efficiency
➜ Reduced unnecessary operating load
➜ Less wear and tear
➜ Reliable compressed air production
➜ Consistent compressor performance
➜ Support for longer equipment service life

Benefits of an Air-Water Separator


Moisture can accumulate in compressed-air pipelines, receiver tanks, and equipment during normal compressor operation. The SJ Air-Water Separator helps remove bulk water from the compressed-air stream, supporting cleaner air distribution and reducing the amount of liquid water reaching downstream equipment.


When correctly installed and maintained, it helps protect pneumatic machinery, supports reliable equipment operation, and reduces the risk of moisture-related maintenance issues.

- Poha and rice processing plants

- Food packaging and sealing industries

- Snack and namkeen manufacturing

- Dairy processing and edible oil packaging

- Fruit and vegetable processing plants

- Seed cleaning and sorting facilities

- Cattle-feed and agricultural processing plants


Installation and Compressed-Air Treatment


Depending on the system design, the separator can be installed after the air compressor or receiver tank or upstream of critical production machinery.


For more effective compressed-air treatment, it can be used in combination with refrigerated air dryers, pre-filters, after-filters, activated carbon filters, and automatic condensate drain valves. The appropriate combination depends on the required air quality, operating pressure, airflow, and application.


Note: An air-water separator is designed to remove bulk liquid water. It does not remove all water vapour or guarantee oil-free compressed air. Additional treatment equipment may be required to meet specific air-quality requirements.

Moisture Removal for Industrial Compressed Air


Compressed air can contain moisture that condenses as the air cools. Without suitable treatment, this moisture may contribute to pipeline corrosion, water accumulation, pneumatic equipment problems, and additional maintenance.


A refrigerated air dryer cools compressed air to condense moisture so it can be separated and drained from the system. This helps supply drier compressed air to downstream equipment. Actual drying performance depends on inlet air temperature, pressure, ambient conditions, airflow, and the dryer's rated operating conditions.


Industrial Applications


The SJ Refrigerated Air Dryer is suitable for compressed-air systems used in:


• Metal mould manufacturing

• Pattern-making industries

• Fabrication workshops

• Forging industries

• Engineering and manufacturing units

• CNC and machine shops

• Pneumatic machinery

• Industrial automation

• Metal processing

• General manufacturing


Pre-Filters and After-Filters


Pre-filters and after-filters can help remove particles and other contaminants from compressed air when selected for the application. Confirm pressure ratings and system compatibility before installation: the stated filter pressure rating is up to 12 Bar, while the dryer is rated for a maximum working pressure of 16 Bar. The complete system must operate within the ratings of all installed components.

Industrial Pressure Drop: The Hidden Cost of Compressed Air Inefficiency


Industrial pressure drop may seem like a minor technical issue, but it can affect energy consumption, production efficiency, equipment performance, and operating costs.


When compressed air loses pressure between the compressor and the point of use, machinery may not receive the pressure it requires. This can lead to inefficient operation and unnecessary energy consumption.


⚠️ How Pressure Drop Affects Industrial Operations


Excessive pressure drop across a compressed-air system can contribute to:


• Increased energy consumption and electricity costs

• Reduced machine performance and production efficiency

• Inconsistent operation of pneumatic equipment

• Additional stress on system components

• Increased maintenance requirements

• Production interruptions and avoidable downtime


🔧 What Causes Pressure Drop?


Pressure losses can occur throughout a compressed-air distribution system. Common causes include:


• Undersized air pipelines

• Poor piping layout and unnecessary bends

• Air leaks at joints, fittings, and connections

• Clogged or incorrectly sized filters

• Pressure losses across dryers and treatment equipment

• Inadequate air receiver capacity or poorly designed storage arrangements

• Excessive airflow demand through restricted sections of the system


Identifying the actual cause is essential before making changes to the compressor or increasing its operating pressure.


✅ How to Improve Compressed-Air System Efficiency


A properly designed and maintained compressed-air system can help reduce avoidable pressure losses and improve performance.


Key measures include:


• Selecting correctly sized pipelines

• Designing an efficient air distribution layout

• Inspecting and repairing air leaks

• Maintaining filters and air dryers

• Monitoring pressure at the compressor and points of use

• Evaluating air receiver capacity and demand fluctuations

• Matching compressor capacity to actual plant requirements

• Keeping operating pressure as low as practical while meeting machinery requirements

Industrial Downtime: More Than a Maintenance Problem


Downtime is never just a repair issue. It directly affects industrial productivity, operating costs, delivery commitments, and customer confidence. When a compressed air system fails or cannot maintain the required pressure, connected machinery may stop, production can slow down, and operational targets can be missed.


What Does Industrial Downtime Really Cost?


1. Lost Production Output

When the compressed air supply stops, pneumatic machinery and production equipment may stop working. Lost production time can affect daily targets, manufacturing schedules, and overall output.


2. Wasted Manpower

Operators, technicians, and supervisors may remain idle while equipment is unavailable, increasing labour costs and reducing workforce productivity.


3. Energy and Restart Losses

Repeated restarts, inefficient operation, and pressure fluctuations can affect energy efficiency and place additional stress on equipment. The actual impact depends on the system design and operating conditions.


4. Delayed Deliveries and Commitments

Production interruptions can delay dispatch schedules and customer orders, affecting delivery performance and long-term business relationships.


5. Higher Emergency Repair Costs

Unexpected breakdowns can require urgent troubleshooting, replacement parts, and unplanned maintenance. Preventive maintenance and timely inspections can identify potential problems before they cause costly interruptions.


How Can Industries Reduce Compressed Air System Downtime?


A reliable compressed air system starts with the right equipment selection, proper system sizing, effective air treatment, sound piping design, and planned maintenance.


Industries can improve system reliability by:

• Scheduling preventive maintenance and regular equipment inspections.

• Checking for air leaks and abnormal pressure drops.

• Selecting compressors according to actual airflow and pressure requirements.

• Maintaining air filters, refrigerated air dryers, and condensate drains.

• Using appropriately sized air receiver tanks and distribution pipelines.

• Monitoring system performance to identify potential issues early.

title: Oil-Free Air Compressor Components | Working & Applications
excerpt: Discover the key components of an oil-free air compressor, including the motor, compression pump, air cleaner, check valve, pressure controls, receiver tank, and drain valve. Learn how these components support clean compressed air delivery for suitable medical, laboratory, pharmaceutical, electronics, and industrial applications.
content:
Understanding Oil-Free Air Compressor Components


Most people use an air compressor without understanding what makes it work reliably. An oil-free air compressor is an engineered system in which each component contributes to air compression, pressure control, and reliable operation.


Unlike oil-lubricated compression designs, an oil-free compressor is designed to prevent lubricating oil from entering the compression chamber. However, the actual air quality depends on the compressor design, intake conditions, and the complete compressed air system.


Key Components of an Oil-Free Air Compressor


1. Electric Motor

The electric motor supplies the mechanical power required to operate the compressor pump and generate compressed air.


2. Compression Pump

The pump draws in atmospheric air and compresses it to the required pressure. Its design determines important operating characteristics, including airflow capacity and compression performance.


3. Air Cleaner or Intake Filter

The intake filter helps prevent dust and airborne particles from entering the compression system, protecting internal components and supporting reliable operation.


4. Check Valve and Unloader Line

The check valve helps prevent compressed air from flowing backwards from the receiver tank. The unloader mechanism releases trapped pressure where required by the compressor design, supporting appropriate starting and stopping operation.


5. Pressure Gauge and Control System

The pressure gauge displays system pressure, while the pressure switch or control panel helps regulate compressor operation according to the system's control settings.


6. Air Receiver Tank

The receiver tank stores compressed air, helps accommodate short-term fluctuations in demand, and reduces frequent compressor cycling in suitable systems.


7. Drain Valve

Moisture can accumulate inside the receiver tank as compressed air cools. The drain valve removes collected condensate and helps protect the tank and downstream equipment from moisture-related problems.


Where Are Oil-Free Air Compressors Used?


Oil-free air compressors are selected for applications where reducing the risk of oil contamination is important, including:


• Medical and healthcare facilities, where the system must meet applicable medical-air requirements.

• Laboratories and research environments.

• Pharmaceutical and cosmetics manufacturing.

• Electronics assembly and precision operations.

• Small workshops, service centers, and suitable industrial applications.


Important: An oil-free compressor does not automatically guarantee sterile, dry, or contaminant-free air. Applications with strict air-quality requirements may need additional filtration, drying, monitoring, and validation to meet the applicable standards.

title: 100-Litre Air Receiver Tank at 8 Bar | Backup Time Explained
excerpt: How long can a 100-litre compressed air receiver tank supply air at 8 bar without a running compressor? The answer depends on the starting pressure, minimum usable pressure, and air consumption. Learn why an air receiver tank acts as a buffer rather than a replacement for compressor capacity.
content:
Most people overestimate air receiver tank backup time, and that is where mistakes begin.


A 100-litre compressed air receiver tank operating at 8 bar cannot provide a fixed backup time without knowing the air consumption and the minimum pressure required by the equipment.


In some operating conditions, the usable air supply may last only around 30 seconds. However, the actual duration depends on the system's starting pressure, the minimum usable pressure, and the connected tools' air consumption.


Why does this happen?


An air receiver tank stores compressed air, providing a buffer that helps manage short-term variations in demand. However, its usable air supply is limited.


What happens when the compressor stops?


• A 100-liter receiver tank has a limited storage capacity.
• At 8 bar gauge pressure, the tank contains more air than it would at atmospheric pressure, but only part of that air may be usable before pressure falls below the equipment's operating requirement.
• Continuous pneumatic tool consumption causes the tank pressure to drop.
• Without the compressor running, the air supply is not replenished.


The result? Depending on air demand and the minimum operating pressure, the available supply may last only seconds.


Common misconception: A bigger air receiver tank means longer backup time.


The reality is that an air receiver tank helps stabilize pressure, accommodate short-term demand peaks, and reduce frequent compressor cycling in suitable systems. It does not replace the compressor's ability to deliver the required airflow continuously.


What should industries focus on?


• Correct compressor sizing based on airflow requirements in CFM.
• Matching compressed air demand with compressor supply capacity.
• Selecting an appropriate air receiver tank based on system requirements.
• Maintaining suitable operating pressure and minimizing pressure drops.
• Evaluating air consumption during peak-demand conditions.


The bottom line: An air receiver tank is a buffer, not a substitute for sufficient compressor capacity.


If production stops shortly after the compressor shuts down, the system may simply lack enough usable stored air to support the connected equipment.

The right solution depends on actual demand, required pressure, and operating conditions.

title: Air Compressor Duty Cycle | Prevent Overheating and Downtime | Sarv jagat
excerpt: Continuous air compressor operation can increase heat buildup, energy consumption, and equipment wear when the system is not designed for the actual air demand. Correct compressor sizing, proper cooling, and suitable load management help maintain reliable performance and reduce the risk of unexpected breakdowns.
content:
Running a compressor continuously may seem productive, but it can indicate a problem when the system is not designed for the actual air demand.


MYTH: An air compressor should run continuously.


FACT: Incorrect sizing, excessive loading, or inadequate cooling can lead to overheating, increased wear, and unexpected breakdowns.


Here is what can happen when an industrial air compressor operates under unsuitable conditions:


• Overheating: Excessive heat can affect operating efficiency and damage components.
• Oil degradation: In oil-lubricated compressors, high operating temperatures can accelerate lubricant deterioration and reduce its effectiveness.
• Increased wear: Prolonged operation under unsuitable conditions can contribute to premature component wear.
• Unexpected breakdowns: Poor system design, inadequate maintenance, or excessive operating loads can increase downtime.


Why does this happen?


When compressed air demand exceeds the compressor's effective supply capacity, the machine may struggle to maintain the required system pressure. Depending on the compressor type and control settings, it may operate for extended periods under load, increasing heat generation and energy consumption.


A compressor running continuously does not automatically mean the system is incorrectly designed. Some industrial compressors are designed for continuous-duty operation. However, constant operation at full load, inability to maintain pressure, or frequent overheating can indicate that the system requires inspection.


Common mistake: Assuming that a running compressor means the entire system is operating correctly.


What should you do instead?


• Match compressor capacity in CFM to actual compressed air demand.
• Check operating pressure and load/unload cycles where applicable.
• Ensure adequate cooling, ventilation, and airflow around the compressor.
• Follow the manufacturer's operating limits and preventive maintenance schedule.
• Inspect for air leaks, pressure drops, and unusually high air consumption.
• Evaluate whether a VFD/VSD compressor is suitable for applications with fluctuating air demand.


Reality check: A compressor running continuously is not necessarily inefficient, but persistent full-load operation, excessive heat, or unstable pressure should not be ignored.


The bottom line: Correct compressor sizing, suitable duty-cycle management, and regular maintenance help support stable output, energy efficiency, and longer equipment life.

How a VFD Works:

title: Sarv Jagat Corporation | Air Compressor Pressure Drop & Pipe Sizing Guide
excerpt: Undersized pipes, long pipelines, bends, fittings, and air leaks can contribute to pressure drop in compressed air systems. Learn how proper compressed air pipe sizing and pipeline design help maintain stable pressure, improve air delivery, and support efficient industrial operations.
content:
Only 1% of technicians get this right… 👇


Question: What causes pressure drop in a compressed air pipeline?

A. Pipe size
B. HP (motor power)


👉 Correct Answer: A. Pipe size ✅


Why? Let’s understand it simply.


Pressure drop is the reduction in air pressure as compressed air travels through pipes, fittings, valves, and other components in a compressed air distribution system. One important cause is resistance to airflow, which depends on pipe diameter, pipeline length, airflow demand, and the design of the distribution network.


What Causes Pressure Drop in a Compressed Air System?


• Smaller pipe diameter: Undersized pipes increase airflow velocity and friction losses, which can contribute to greater pressure drop.

• Long pipelines: The longer the compressed air has to travel, the greater the potential for friction-related pressure loss.

• Bends, joints, and fittings: Elbows, valves, connectors, and other restrictions add resistance to airflow.

• Air leaks: Leaks waste compressed air and can cause system pressure to fall when the compressor cannot keep up with demand.

• High air demand: When multiple machines consume compressed air simultaneously, an undersized distribution system may struggle to deliver the required airflow at the necessary pressure.


Does Compressor HP Cause Pressure Drop?


Motor horsepower (HP) does not directly determine pressure drop in the pipeline. HP indicates the motor's power rating, while the compressor's airflow capacity, operating pressure, and the design of the compressed air distribution system determine whether the required air can reach the equipment effectively.


Even a high-HP industrial air compressor may struggle to maintain the required pressure at a machine if the piping is undersized or poorly designed.


How Can You Reduce Pressure Drop?


✔ Select the correct compressed air pipe diameter based on airflow demand and pipeline length.
✔ Design the pipeline layout to minimize unnecessary bends and restrictions.
✔ Check joints, fittings, valves, and connections for leaks.
✔ Maintain air filters, dryers, and other treatment components according to their service requirements.
✔ Measure pressure at the compressor outlet and critical points of use to identify where losses occur.
✔ Ensure the compressor, air receiver, and distribution network are suitable for the application's airflow and pressure requirements.


Why Is Proper Air Pipeline Design Important?

What Goes Wrong When You Focus Only on HP?


Choosing a compressor based on horsepower alone can result in:


• Overspending on equipment that does not match actual air demand

• Insufficient or inefficient air delivery

title: Sarv Jagat Corporation | How to Calculate Actual Air Compressor CFM
excerpt: Rated CFM does not always represent the actual compressed air output available in your plant. Learn how to estimate real air compressor CFM using an air receiver tank volume, pressure difference, and filling time. Understanding actual compressor airflow helps industries evaluate performance, identify system inefficiencies, and make better compressed air system sizing decisions.
content:
Check the REAL CFM of Your Air Compressor—Not Just the Nameplate Value.


In industrial environments, compressor performance problems do not always come from machine failure. Sometimes, they come from incorrect assumptions about actual airflow capacity.


Many industries rely only on the rated CFM mentioned on an air compressor nameplate or datasheet. However, the actual air delivery available under plant operating conditions can differ due to operating pressure, temperature, system losses, air leakage, and changing air demand.


Understanding the difference between rated airflow and measured compressor output is essential for maintaining an efficient compressed air system.


How to Calculate Actual Air Compressor CFM


A simplified air receiver filling method can be used to estimate compressor airflow.


Formula:

CFM = (V × ΔP) ÷ (T × 14.7)


Where:

• V = Air receiver tank volume in cubic feet (ft³)
• ΔP = Pressure increase in PSI
• T = Time taken in minutes
• 14.7 = Approximate atmospheric pressure at sea level in PSI


Example Calculation


Consider the following air compressor testing values:


• Tank volume: 500 liters = 17.66 ft³
• Pressure increase: 16 bar = 232.06 PSI
• Filling time: 4 minutes 20 seconds = 4.33 minutes


Calculation:


CFM = (17.66 × 232.06) ÷ (4.33 × 14.7)


Estimated Airflow = 64.38 CFM


This result assumes the receiver pressure rises from 0 to 16 bar gauge during the test, with no air consumption or leakage.


For an accurate field measurement, record both initial and final tank pressures. The pressure difference must be used in the calculation.


Temperature changes, leakage, air consumption during testing, and other test conditions can also affect the result.


What Does Actual CFM Tell You?


If your production equipment requires more airflow than your compressor can deliver, the system may struggle to maintain the required operating pressure.


This can lead to:


• Pressure fluctuations
• Reduced machine efficiency
• Higher energy consumption
• Increased compressor operating load
• Unexpected production downtime


Reality Check: Rated CFM vs Actual Airflow


Rated CFM, or Free Air Delivery (FAD), is determined under specified test conditions and standards. Actual performance in an industrial plant can vary depending on operating pressure, inlet conditions, temperature, maintenance condition, and system configuration.


Your plant has real operating conditions, including heat, air leakage, pressure losses, and variable demand.


If actual compressor airflow is not evaluated, equipment selection and system planning may be based on incorrect assumptions.


Why Is Measuring Actual CFM Important?


✔ Evaluate actual compressor performance.
✔ Identify potential airflow deficiencies.
✔ Check whether compressor capacity matches production demand.
✔ Avoid incorrect compressed air system sizing.
✔ Identify opportunities to reduce energy waste.
✔ Support stable pressure and reliable production operations.


Sarv Jagat Approach


At Sarv Jagat Corporation, we focus on real performance data rather than assumptions. Our approach to industrial compressed air solutions considers actual airflow requirements, operating pressure, compressor capacity, and system design.


From industrial air compressor selection to compressed air system planning and installation, understanding real operating requirements helps businesses build reliable and efficient systems.


In industry, small miscalculations can lead to big operational losses.

excerpt: Industrial air compressor failures are often linked to incorrect selection, poor installation, inadequate ventilation, contamination, and neglected preventive maintenance. content:
Most compressor failures are not necessarily caused by manufacturing defects. Many result from incorrect equipment selection, poor installation, unsuitable operating conditions, or inadequate maintenance practices.


In industrial environments, compressed air is often treated as a background utility. However, when an air compressor fails, the impact extends far beyond the machine. It can affect plant uptime, production quality, energy consumption, equipment performance, and delivery commitments.


Understanding the common causes of industrial air compressor failure is the first step toward reducing operational risks and improving equipment reliability.


Common Causes of Industrial Air Compressor Failure


• Incorrect Duty Cycle Selection: Selecting a compressor that does not match the application's operating hours and actual air demand can place unnecessary stress on the equipment.

• Improper System Sizing: Incorrect compressor capacity, unsuitable pressure settings, and frequent loading and unloading can contribute to inefficient operation and excessive cycling.

• Poor Installation and Ventilation: Restricted airflow, inadequate ventilation, and insufficient heat dissipation can cause elevated operating temperatures.

• Moisture and Contamination: Improper air treatment, oil carryover, and particle contamination can affect compressor components and downstream pneumatic equipment.

• Neglected Preventive Maintenance: Delayed filter replacement, incorrect lubrication practices, blocked coolers, and missed service intervals can increase the risk of equipment failure.

• Ignoring Early Warning Signs: Pressure instability, rising operating temperature, unusual noise, vibration, and increased power consumption may indicate developing problems.


Why Do Compressor Problems Become Major Failures?


Most compressor problems develop gradually. Small issues such as restricted cooling airflow, air leaks, contaminated filters, or incorrect operating pressure may initially go unnoticed.


Over time, these conditions can increase energy consumption, reduce operating efficiency, accelerate component wear, and eventually cause unexpected shutdowns.


Regular inspections, performance monitoring, correct operating settings, and scheduled preventive maintenance help identify potential problems before they become major production interruptions.


How Sarv Jagat Corporation Approaches Compressor Reliability


At Sarv Jagat Corporation, we focus on engineering compressed air systems around actual industrial requirements, with attention to:


• Correct compressor selection based on CFM, pressure, and duty cycle

• Proper system sizing and application matching

• Suitable installation, ventilation, and cooling arrangements

• Appropriate filtration, moisture separation, and air drying

The reality is simple: compressor reliability depends on the complete compressed air system, not just the machine.

Energy Efficiency in Compressed Air Systems—Reduce Power Consumption and Operating Costs


Energy efficiency in compressed air systems is not optional. It directly affects your monthly electricity bill, production efficiency, and long-term operating costs.


Compressed air is one of the most energy-intensive utilities in an industrial plant. Since compressors often operate for extended hours, even small inefficiencies can lead to significant energy losses over time. Air leaks, pressure drops, incorrect compressor selection, and poor maintenance can increase power consumption without improving production output.


Common Causes of Energy Loss in Compressed Air Systems


Several factors can reduce the energy efficiency of an industrial compressed air system:


• Undetected Air Leaks: Leaks in pipelines, joints, valves, and pneumatic connections waste compressed air and force compressors to work longer.

• Pressure Drops: Incorrect pipe sizing, long pipelines, clogged filters, and unsuitable accessories can restrict airflow and create unnecessary pressure losses.

• Incorrect Compressor Selection: An oversized compressor may consume more energy than required, while an undersized system may struggle to meet actual air demand.

• Moisture and Contamination: Poor air treatment and clogged filters can affect airflow, equipment performance, and system reliability.

• Inadequate Preventive Maintenance: Dirty coolers, blocked filters, worn components, and neglected servicing can increase operating costs.


How to Improve Compressed Air System Efficiency


An energy-efficient compressed air system requires proper engineering, correct equipment selection, and regular monitoring.


✔ Correct Compressor Sizing: Select compressor capacity according to actual CFM demand, operating pressure, and production requirements.


✔ Air Leak Detection: Inspect pipelines, fittings, valves, and connections to reduce unnecessary compressed air losses.


✔ Stable Operating Pressure: Design suitable piping and select correctly sized accessories to minimise pressure drops.


✔ Proper Air Treatment: Use suitable air dryers, moisture separators, and filtration systems to maintain the required compressed air quality.


✔ Preventive Maintenance: Keep coolers clean, filters in good condition, and compressor components properly maintained.


✔ Demand-Based Compressor Selection: Consider fixed-speed or VFD/VSD compressor technology according to the plant's air consumption pattern and load variations.


Why System Engineering Matters


Energy efficiency does not come from selecting a compressor alone. It depends on the complete compressed air system, including compressor capacity, operating pressure, air distribution, filtration, drying, accessories, and maintenance practices.


An oversized compressor can waste energy, while an undersized system may struggle to maintain the required pressure. Poorly selected accessories and neglected maintenance can further increase operating costs.

Our objective is to help industries improve compressed air system performance, manage energy consumption, and maintain reliable operation through proper system selection and engineering.


Efficient compressed air systems do not save energy only during an audit. They help reduce energy waste throughout everyday industrial operations.

Piston vs Screw vs Oil-Free Air Compressor—Which One Is Right for Your Industry?


Let's simplify industrial air compressors in the most practical way possible!


Every compressor type has its own working style, advantages, and ideal applications. Choosing the wrong compressor for your production requirements can lead to unnecessary energy consumption, higher maintenance costs, pressure fluctuations, and operational challenges.


Understanding the difference between a piston compressor, screw compressor, and oil-free compressor is the first step towards building an efficient compressed air system.


1. Piston Air Compressor—The Hardworking Traditional Performer


A piston compressor is a practical and rugged solution for applications that require compressed air intermittently or at comparatively lower capacities.


Its personality: Hardworking, straightforward, and dependable.


• Uses a reciprocating piston mechanism to compress air.

• Suitable for workshops, garages, small manufacturing units, and intermittent pneumatic applications.

• Available in different capacities and pressure configurations.

• Often has a comparatively lower initial investment.

• Requires periodic maintenance of valves, piston rings, lubrication systems, and other components.

• Can produce higher noise and vibration than many rotary screw models.


Best suited for: Workshops, service stations, small production units, and applications with intermittent air demand.


Some piston compressors are also designed for demanding duty cycles. Always check the manufacturer's rated operating conditions before selecting one for continuous operation.


2. Screw Air Compressor—The Continuous Production Professional


A rotary screw compressor uses two rotating screw elements to compress air and is widely used in industrial applications requiring a steady compressed air supply.


Its personality: Smooth, professional, and production-focused.


• Designed for applications requiring a sustained compressed air supply.

• Provides consistent airflow when correctly sized for the demand.

• Generally operates with lower pulsation and often lower noise than comparable reciprocating systems.

• Suitable for manufacturing plants, fabrication units, food processing, textile industries, and industrial automation.

• Available in fixed-speed and VFD/VSD configurations.

• Requires scheduled servicing, including attention to oil, filters, coolers, and other components in oil-injected models.


Best suited for: Manufacturing facilities, continuous production lines, fabrication, textile processing, and industries with regular compressed air demand.


VFD/VSD advantage: Variable-speed technology can help reduce energy consumption when air demand fluctuates, depending on the plant's load profile and system design.


3. Oil-Free Air Compressor – The Air Purity Specialist


Oil-free compressors are designed to avoid introducing lubricating oil into the compression chamber, making them suitable for applications with strict compressed air purity requirements.


Its personality: Clean, precise, and quality-conscious.


• Designed for applications requiring oil-free compressed air.

• Suitable for selected pharmaceutical, food processing, electronics, medical, and specialized manufacturing applications.

• Helps avoid contamination from compressor lubricating oil in the compression process.

• Requires application-specific air quality assessment and suitable downstream treatment.

• May involve a higher initial investment depending on technology and capacity.


Best suited for: Applications where oil contamination must be controlled according to the required compressed air quality standards.


An oil-free compressor alone does not guarantee complete compressed air purity. Moisture, particles, and microbiological contamination may also need to be controlled through suitable filtration, drying, system design, and testing.


The Reality: Choosing the Wrong Compressor Can Increase Operating Costs


Many industries do not necessarily choose the wrong machine. They select equipment without fully understanding their actual application requirements.


This can lead to several operational problems:


• Energy Waste: Incorrect compressor sizing or unsuitable control technology can increase electricity consumption.

• Pressure Drops: Poor pipeline design, undersized accessories, and clogged filters can affect pressure at the point of use.

• Frequent Maintenance: Operating equipment outside its recommended conditions can increase component wear.

• Product Quality Issues: Inadequate compressed air treatment can affect processes that require controlled air quality.


How to Select the Right Industrial Air Compressor


The right compressor is not selected by horsepower or purchase price alone. A proper selection considers four essential factors:


1. Application: Understand which machines and processes will use compressed air.


2. Duty Cycle: Determine whether the requirement is intermittent, variable, or continuous.


3. Air Quality: Identify the required oil, moisture, and particle control for the application.


4. System Design: Evaluate CFM demand, operating pressure in bar, pipeline sizing, air receiver capacity, dryers, filters, and future production requirements.

No FRL, More Risk—Why FRL Units Matter in Compressed Air Systems


Most industries invest significantly in industrial air compressors, pneumatic tools, and production machinery but often overlook a small yet important component of the compressed air system: the FRL unit.


FRL stands for Filter, Regulator, and Lubricator. It is commonly installed in pneumatic air supply lines to help condition compressed air before it reaches air-operated equipment.


When the required air treatment and pressure control are missing, moisture, dust, pressure variations, and inadequate lubrication can affect pneumatic equipment performance and increase maintenance requirements.


What Happens When You Ignore FRL in a Pneumatic System?


Operating pneumatic equipment without suitable air preparation can create several problems:


• Moisture-Related Damage: Liquid water in compressed air lines can cause corrosion and affect pneumatic components.

• Rust and Corrosion: Moisture and contaminants can reduce the service life of pipelines, valves, and connected equipment.

• Unstable Operating Pressure: Incorrect pressure regulation can affect pneumatic tool performance and machine operation.

• Insufficient Lubrication: Pneumatic components designed to operate with lubricated air may experience increased friction and wear when lubrication is inadequate.

• Frequent Equipment Problems: Contaminated air and unsuitable operating conditions can increase maintenance requirements and production interruptions.

• Higher Operating Costs: Avoidable repairs, component replacement, and downtime can increase long-term operating expenses.


Understanding the Three Components of an FRL Unit


An FRL unit combines three important air preparation functions.


1. Filter—Removes Contaminants


The filter helps remove solid particles and separates liquid water and other contaminants from compressed air, depending on the filter design and filtration rating.


Key benefits:

• Helps protect pneumatic valves and tools from particles.

• Separates liquid condensate.

• Supports cleaner compressed air at the point of use.

• Reduces contamination-related equipment problems.


2. Regulator—Controls Air Pressure


The regulator controls downstream air pressure according to the required operating setting. It helps maintain suitable working pressure for pneumatic equipment when correctly selected and sized.


Key benefits:

• Helps maintain the required operating pressure.

• Supports consistent pneumatic equipment performance.

• Prevents unnecessarily high downstream pressure.

• Helps match air pressure to application requirements.


3. Lubricator—Supplies Controlled Lubrication


A lubricator introduces a controlled quantity of oil into the compressed air stream for pneumatic components designed to require lubrication.


Key benefits:

• Provides lubrication to compatible pneumatic components.

• Helps reduce friction and wear.

• Supports smooth movement of air-operated equipment.

• Can help extend component service life when used according to manufacturer recommendations.


Important: Not every pneumatic tool or machine requires an air-line lubricator. Some equipment is designed for oil-free operation or has permanent lubrication. Always follow the equipment manufacturer's instructions.


Why Proper Compressed Air Treatment Matters


Compressed air coming directly from a compressor may contain moisture, particles, and oil-related contaminants depending on the compressor type and system configuration.


An FRL unit is a point-of-use air preparation device, not a complete compressed air treatment system. Industrial installations may also require refrigerated air dryers, moisture separators, pre-filters, after-filters, fine filters, and other treatment equipment according to the required air quality.


Proper compressor selection, air drying, filtration, pressure regulation, and pipeline design work together to support reliable pneumatic operations.


Common Industries That Use FRL Units


FRL units are widely used in pneumatic applications across different industries, including:


• CNC and VMC machine operations

• Automotive manufacturing and assembly lines

• Fabrication and metalworking workshops

• Packaging and processing machinery

• Textile manufacturing

• Food and agricultural processing equipment

• Industrial automation and pneumatic control systems


The correct FRL size and configuration depend on airflow demand, operating pressure, connection size, filtration requirements, and the pneumatic equipment being used.

We understand that every component has a role in maintaining compressed air system performance. Proper air treatment and suitable accessories help industries protect pneumatic equipment, manage operating pressure, and improve overall system reliability.


The bottom line: An FRL unit is a small component with an important role in pneumatic air preparation. The right air treatment and pressure control can help reduce avoidable equipment wear, maintenance requirements, and operating costs.

title: Sarv Jagat Corporation | Brochure CFM vs Actual Air Compressor CFM
excerpt: Is your air compressor delivering the CFM mentioned in its brochure? Understand how temperature, atmospheric pressure, altitude, humidity, voltage, and operating conditions affect compressor performance and actual air delivery in industrial environments.
content:
Brochure CFM vs Actual CFM—What Is Your Air Compressor Really Delivering?


Most industries trust the CFM mentioned in an air compressor brochure. But there is an important question that often gets overlooked:


At what operating conditions is that CFM measured?


Compressed air output is influenced by several operating and environmental conditions. The airflow capacity specified in a compressor brochure may be measured under defined test conditions, but actual performance at an industrial plant can vary depending on installation conditions, inlet air quality, operating pressure, and compressor design.


Ignoring these factors can lead to incorrect compressor selection, insufficient airflow, pressure fluctuations, and unnecessary energy consumption.


What Factors Affect Actual Compressor CFM?


Understanding these factors helps industries evaluate compressor performance more accurately.


1. Temperature—Hot Air Affects Air Density


Temperature plays an important role in compressor intake conditions.


• Higher inlet air temperature reduces air density.

• Lower air density means less air mass enters the compressor for the same intake volume.

• High ambient temperatures can also affect compressor cooling and operating performance.


Proper ventilation and suitable compressor installation conditions help maintain reliable operation.


2. Atmospheric Pressure and Altitude – Location Matters


Atmospheric pressure decreases as altitude increases. This affects the density of air entering the compressor.


• Higher-altitude locations have lower atmospheric pressure.

• Lower intake air density can reduce compressor mass-flow capacity.

• Compressor performance should be evaluated using the manufacturer's altitude correction data where applicable.


This is particularly important when selecting industrial air compressors for plants located at higher elevations.


3. Humidity—Moisture in Intake Air


Humidity affects the composition and density of atmospheric air.


• Humid air contains more water vapour and less dry-air mass at the same temperature and pressure.

• Moisture can condense inside compressed air systems as air cools.

• Proper moisture separation and air drying help protect downstream equipment and maintain the required compressed air quality.


Humidity should be considered along with temperature and atmospheric pressure when evaluating intake conditions.


4. Voltage and Electrical Supply – Motor Performance Matters


The electrical supply also influences compressor operation.


• Voltage outside the motor's permitted range can affect motor current, heating, and performance.

• Voltage imbalance and poor electrical connections can increase electrical stress.

• An improperly configured electrical supply may cause protective trips or operating problems.


However, low voltage does not automatically result in a predictable reduction in CFM. Actual airflow depends on motor characteristics, compressor loading, control systems, and operating conditions.


Why Brochure CFM and Actual Air Delivery Can Differ


A compressor's advertised CFM must be understood in relation to its measurement standard and specified test conditions.


Different airflow ratings may refer to different measurements, including:


• Displacement CFM: Theoretical air volume displaced by the compressor's compression elements.

• FAD (Free Air Delivery): Actual delivered air expressed as an equivalent volume at specified inlet reference conditions.

• Operating Airflow: Air delivered under the actual operating pressure and installation conditions.


These values are not interchangeable.


When comparing industrial air compressors, always check the specified FAD, operating pressure, test standard, inlet conditions, and manufacturer's performance data.


What Happens When Actual Airflow Is Lower Than Required?


If a compressor cannot meet the plant's actual air demand, several operational problems may occur:


• Pressure Drops: Insufficient airflow can cause pressure to fall when multiple machines operate simultaneously.

• Machine Inefficiency: Pneumatic equipment may not receive the airflow required for proper operation.

• Energy Waste: Poor compressor selection and system design can increase operating costs.

• Production Instability: Inconsistent compressed air supply can affect machine cycles and production output.

-*Increased Equipment Stress: Continuous operation beyond the intended capacity can place additional demands on the compressor system.


What Should You Ask Before Selecting an Air Compressor?


Instead of asking only, "How much CFM does this compressor deliver?" ask:


"What is the actual free air delivery at my required operating pressure and under which reference conditions?"


Before selecting a compressor, evaluate:


• Required airflow in CFM

• Operating pressure in bar

• Manufacturer-specified FAD and test conditions

• Ambient and inlet air temperature

• Site altitude and atmospheric pressure

• Electrical supply conditions

• Operating hours and duty cycle

• Future production requirements


These details help ensure that the selected compressor matches the actual compressed air demand of the plant.

What Really Matters When Selecting an Air Compressor?

• Air Demand (CFM): Understand the total compressed air consumption of connected machinery and equipment.

• Working Pressure (Bar/PSI): Identify the pressure required by the application, including any pressure losses across the system.

• Duty Cycle: Evaluate operating hours, load variations, and whether the compressor needs to support continuous or intermittent demand.

• Air Quality Requirements: Determine whether the application requires dry air, particulate filtration, oil-vapour reduction, or an oil-free compression process.

• System Losses: Consider pressure drops, air leakage, undersized pipelines, and inefficient distribution.


Selecting equipment without evaluating these factors can result in an unsuitable compressed air installation.


Engineering Factors Behind Proper Compressor Selection


A reliable compressed air system begins with accurate planning and application-based calculations.


Important considerations include:


✔ Actual Air Consumption: Calculate the air demand of machinery instead of relying on estimated requirements.


✔ Peak and Average Demand: Understand variations in consumption to select suitable compressor capacity and control technology.


✔ Pressure Drop Analysis: Evaluate losses across pipelines, filters, dryers, fittings, and distribution networks.


✔ Application-Specific Air Quality: Select appropriate air treatment equipment according to the required air quality, including refrigerated dryers, pre-filters, fine filters, micro-filters, and activated carbon filters where necessary.


✔ Future Expansion Planning: Consider expected production growth and additional machinery when designing the compressed air system.


Every component should be selected to work together according to the plant's operating conditions.


What Happens When an Air Compressor Is Incorrectly Selected?

Industrial plants rarely operate under ideal conditions. Multiple machines may run simultaneously, air demand can fluctuate throughout the day, and long pipeline networks can create pressure losses. Heat, dust, and moisture can also influence equipment performance and compressed air quality.

Why Do Compressed Air Systems Perform Differently in Real Industries?


A compressor's rated specifications provide important information, but selecting equipment based only on its HP, CFM, or maximum pressure does not guarantee that the complete system will meet production requirements.


Real industrial environments involve several operating challenges:


• Fluctuating Air Demand: Different machines consume different amounts of compressed air, and their operating cycles may change throughout the day.

• Multiple Machines Running Simultaneously: Combined air consumption can increase significantly when several production machines operate together.

• Pressure Drops in Pipelines: Long pipelines, undersized piping, fittings, filters, and other restrictions can reduce pressure at the point of use.

• High Operating Temperatures: Ambient heat and inadequate ventilation can affect compressor cooling and operating conditions.

• Dust and Contamination: Industrial environments can introduce contaminants that affect air intake, filtration, and equipment maintenance.

• Moisture in Compressed Air: Compression produces moisture that must be managed through suitable separation, drying, and condensate removal.


These factors must be evaluated before finalizing a compressor and air treatment configuration.


What Happens When a System Is Not Designed for Actual Plant Conditions?


An incorrectly sized or poorly configured compressed air system may experience:


• Pressure instability during peak production

• Higher energy consumption

• Frequent compressor loading and unloading

• Increased maintenance requirements

• Moisture-related problems in pneumatic equipment

• Reduced machine efficiency

• Unexpected production interruptions


The problem may not be the compressor alone. It can also originate from inadequate air treatment, incorrect pipeline sizing, poor distribution, or a mismatch between air supply and actual demand.


What Does Proper Compressed Air System Design Require?


A reliable industrial compressed air system must be planned around the complete production environment.


Important engineering considerations include:


✔ Real Load Conditions: Analyze actual air consumption, operating hours, machine cycles, and variations in demand.


✔ Proper System Sizing: Select compressor capacity according to measured or calculated airflow requirements and the required working pressure.


✔ Pressure Drop Evaluation: Consider pipeline length, diameter, fittings, filters, dryers, and distribution layout.


✔ Stable Pressure Delivery: Configure suitable compressor controls and distribution systems to support the required pressure at the point of use.


✔ Appropriate Air Treatment: Select moisture separators, refrigerated dryers, and filtration equipment according to the required compressed air quality.

content:
FRL Unit – Filter, Regulator, and Lubricator in Compressed Air Systems


Compressed air is useful for industrial machinery only when its pressure and quality meet the requirements of the application.


In pneumatic systems, an FRL unit (Filter, Regulator, Lubricator) is commonly used to condition compressed air before it enters pneumatic tools, cylinders, valves, and other equipment.


An FRL assembly combines three functions: filtration, pressure regulation, and lubrication. Depending on the equipment and application, all three components may be used together or selected individually.


What Are the Components of an FRL Unit?


An FRL system generally consists of the following components:


1. Air Filter


The air filter removes solid particles such as dust, dirt, and other contaminants from compressed air. Depending on its design, it can also separate collected liquid water and help protect downstream pneumatic components.


Key functions:

• Removes solid contaminants from compressed air

• Separates liquid condensate within its rated capability

• Helps protect pneumatic valves, cylinders, and tools

• Supports cleaner air at the point of use


Note: A standard FRL filter does not replace a properly sized compressed air dryer. A dryer is required when the application needs control of water vapour and pressure dew point.


2. Pressure Regulator


The pressure regulator controls the downstream air pressure supplied to pneumatic equipment.


It helps maintain the required operating pressure when inlet pressure or air demand changes, within the regulator's specified operating range.


Key functions:

• Adjusts outlet pressure according to equipment requirements

• Helps maintain stable downstream pressure

• Supports consistent pneumatic equipment operation

• Prevents supplying unnecessarily high pressure to equipment


3. Lubricator


A pneumatic lubricator introduces a controlled quantity of oil mist into the compressed air stream.


This lubrication can reduce friction and wear in pneumatic equipment specifically designed to operate with lubricated air.


Key functions:

• Supplies controlled lubrication to compatible pneumatic components

• Helps reduce friction in moving parts

• Supports equipment designed for air-line lubrication

• Can help reduce wear when used according to manufacturer requirements


Important: Not every pneumatic machine requires an air-line lubricator. Some equipment is designed for oil-free operation or has permanent lubrication. Always follow the equipment manufacturer's recommendations.


4. Pressure Gauge


A pressure gauge is commonly fitted to the regulator to display downstream operating pressure.


Key functions:

• Shows the regulated air pressure

• Helps operators monitor system conditions

• Supports pressure adjustment

• Makes routine inspection easier


Why Is an FRL Unit Important in Pneumatic Systems?


When correctly selected and maintained, an FRL assembly helps prepare compressed air for connected equipment.


Its benefits include:


✔ Equipment Protection: Filtration helps reduce contamination entering pneumatic components.

✔ Pressure Management: Regulation helps supply suitable operating pressure to machinery and tools.

✔ Controlled Lubrication: A lubricator supports equipment that requires air-line lubrication.

✔ Reliable Operation: Proper air conditioning helps pneumatic equipment operate within its specified requirements.

✔ Maintenance Support: Correct filtration and pressure settings can help reduce avoidable wear and servicing needs.


Where Are FRL Units Used?


FRL units are commonly used in:


• Pneumatic automation systems

• CNC and VMC machine applications

• Industrial assembly lines

• Pneumatic cylinders and actuators

• Packaging machinery

• Industrial pneumatic tools

• Manufacturing and fabrication equipment


The correct FRL size and configuration depend on airflow consumption, operating pressure, connection size, air quality requirements, and the manufacturer's specifications.


FRL Unit vs Complete Compressed Air Treatment System


An FRL unit provides point-of-use air preparation near pneumatic machinery. However, it is not a complete compressed air treatment solution for an entire industrial plant.


A complete compressed air system may also require:


• Moisture Separators: To remove bulk liquid water from compressed air.

• Refrigerated Air Dryers: To reduce water vapour and achieve the required pressure dew point.

• Pre-Filters and After-Filters: To remove contaminants according to the required filtration level.

• Fine and Micro-Filters: For applications requiring finer particle and aerosol filtration.

• Activated Carbon Filters: To reduce oil vapour and odour where required.

title: Sarv Jagat Corporation | VFD Technology – Working, Benefits & Safety
excerpt: A Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) controls AC motor speed by adjusting supply frequency and voltage. Learn how VFD technology works, its industrial advantages, energy-saving potential, and essential installation safety practices.
content:
VFD Technology—Working Principle, Industrial Benefits, and Safety


Energy efficiency and precise motor control are important requirements in modern industrial systems. A Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) is an electronic device used to control the speed and torque of an AC motor by adjusting the frequency and voltage supplied to it.


Instead of operating motors at a constant speed, VFD technology allows industries to adjust motor operation according to actual process requirements.


VFDs are widely used in industrial machinery, pumps, fans, conveyors, manufacturing equipment, and variable-speed screw air compressors.


What Is a VFD?


A variable frequency drive is an electronic motor controller that regulates the speed of an AC motor by changing the frequency of its electrical supply.


Motor speed is directly related to supply frequency and the number of motor poles. By controlling the output frequency, a VFD can adjust motor speed to suit the application.


In industrial compressed air systems, VFD technology can help match compressor output with changing air demand.


How Does a VFD Work?


A typical VFD operates through four main stages:


1. AC Input Supply: The drive receives electrical power from an AC supply.

2. Rectifier: The rectifier converts incoming AC power into DC power.

3. DC Bus: Capacitors and associated components stabilize and filter the DC voltage.

4. Inverter: Power electronic switches convert DC power into variable-frequency AC output to control the motor.


By adjusting the output frequency and voltage according to the drive's control strategy, the VFD regulates motor speed.


Key Advantages of VFD Technology


VFDs offer several benefits when correctly selected and configured for the application:


• Energy Efficiency: Potentially reduces energy consumption in variable-load applications by matching motor speed to actual demand.

• Smooth Starting and Stopping: Controlled acceleration and deceleration can reduce starting current and mechanical shock compared with direct-on-line starting.

• Precise Speed Control: Allows motor speed to be adjusted according to process requirements.

• Reduced Mechanical Stress: Controlled starting and speed changes can reduce stress on connected machinery.

• Process Control: Helps maintain suitable operating conditions in applications requiring variable motor speed.

• Operational Flexibility: Supports changing production requirements through adjustable motor control.


Actual energy savings depend on the application, load profile, motor characteristics, drive settings, and overall system design.


Where Are VFDs Used in Industries?


Variable Frequency Drives are commonly used in:


• Industrial screw air compressors

• Water pumps and booster systems

• Industrial ventilation fans

• Conveyor systems

• Manufacturing machinery

• Packaging and processing equipment

• HVAC systems

• Industrial automation systems


In VFD screw compressors, motor speed can be adjusted according to compressed air demand within the compressor's designed operating range. This can help reduce unnecessary unloading operations and improve energy management when demand fluctuates.


Important VFD Installation and Safety Considerations


Correct installation and configuration are essential for safe and reliable VFD operation.


Important precautions include:


• Proper Earthing: Follow the manufacturer's grounding and earthing requirements.

• Suitable Motor Cables: Use correctly rated cables and shielded motor cables where required by the drive manufacturer and installation design.

• Correct Parameters: Configure motor nameplate data, acceleration and deceleration times, protection settings, and control parameters before operation.

• Output-Side Protection: Never connect VFD output directly to an MCB or switchgear as a substitute for a properly designed motor circuit. Output-side devices must be selected and installed according to the VFD manufacturer's instructions.

• Electrical Isolation: Isolate the power supply and allow the DC bus capacitors to discharge for the specified time before servicing. Verify that the equipment is de-energised.

• Qualified Installation: Installation, commissioning, and maintenance should be carried out by trained electrical personnel.


Always follow the VFD manufacturer's installation manual and applicable electrical safety standards.


VFD Technology in Compressed Air Systems


In industrial compressed air applications, air consumption often changes throughout the production cycle. A fixed-speed compressor generally operates according to its control and loading arrangement, while a VFD/VSD compressor can vary motor speed to respond to changing air demand.


A properly selected variable-speed compressor system can offer:


• Better matching of compressor output with changing air demand

• Improved pressure management

• Potential reduction in energy consumption under variable-load conditions

• Reduced unnecessary running

• Greater flexibility in industrial operations


The compressor must still be selected according to actual CFM requirements, working pressure, duty cycle, and operating conditions.

Correct compressor selection begins with understanding actual air consumption and required working pressure.


2. Air Dryer for Moisture Removal


During compression, air temperature increases, and moisture can condense as the air cools.


A refrigerated air dryer reduces water vapour content by cooling compressed air and removing condensed moisture. The correct dryer must be selected according to airflow, inlet temperature, operating pressure, and ambient conditions.


3. Filtration System for Compressed Air Quality


Compressed air may contain solid particles, water aerosols, and oil contaminants depending on the compressor and system conditions.


Suitable filtration equipment helps remove contaminants according to the required air quality.


Common filtration options include:


• Pre-filters

• After-filters

• Fine filters

• Micro-filters

• Activated carbon filters


Each filter serves a different purpose and should be selected according to the application and required filtration level.


4. Air Receiver Tank for Storage and Pressure Stability


An air receiver tank stores compressed air and helps manage short-term variations in demand.


It can reduce rapid compressor cycling when correctly sized and configured, provide a reserve of compressed air, and support more stable system operation.


Receiver tank capacity should be selected according to compressor output, demand patterns, control strategy, and applicable safety requirements.


5. Efficient Piping and Air Distribution


Even a correctly selected compressor may not deliver the required pressure at every machine if the distribution network is poorly designed.


Pipeline diameter, length, fittings, valves, and flow restrictions influence pressure drop.


A properly designed distribution network helps deliver compressed air efficiently to different points of use.


6. Integrated System Engineering


All components must be designed to operate together.


This includes compressor capacity, dryer sizing, filtration stages, receiver tank volume, pressure settings, condensate management, and pipeline configuration.


A mismatch between any of these elements can affect the overall performance of the installation.


What Happens When One Component Is Ignored?


An incomplete or poorly configured compressed air system can lead to:


• Pressure fluctuations during production

• Excessive pressure drops across pipelines

• Moisture-related problems in pneumatic machinery

• Contamination in compressed air lines

• Unnecessary energy consumption

• Frequent maintenance requirements

• Reduced production efficiency


These problems cannot always be solved by installing a larger compressor. The complete system must be evaluated to identify the actual cause.


Why Is Complete System Engineering Important?


A properly engineered compressed air system considers the entire production environment rather than focusing on compressor capacity alone.


Important factors include:


✔ Actual air consumption and peak demand

✔ Required working pressure at the point of use

✔ Compressor type and operating duty cycle

✔ Correct dryer and filter selection

✔ Receiver tank sizing and pressure management

✔ Pipeline layout and pressure drop calculations

✔ Future production expansion requirements


When these factors are considered together, industries can build compressed air systems that better match their operating requirements.

title: Sarv Jagat Corporation | When Production Grows, Your Air System Must Grow
excerpt: As factories expand and production capacity increases, existing compressed air systems may struggle to meet growing air demand. Learn the warning signs of an undersized compressed air system and why capacity evaluation and system upgrades are important for industrial efficiency.
content:
When Production Grows, Your Compressed Air System Must Grow


Industries evolve, production capacity increases, and new machines become part of manufacturing operations. However, many factories continue using the same compressed air system that was originally designed for a smaller production capacity.


As additional machinery is installed, total air consumption increases. An existing compressor, dryer, receiver tank, and pipeline network may no longer be suitable for the plant's updated requirements.


This mismatch can affect production performance, energy consumption, and the reliability of the entire compressed air system.


At Sarv Jagat Corporation, we believe compressed air infrastructure should be evaluated whenever industrial production expands.


Signs That Your Factory Has Outgrown Its Compressed Air System


An existing compressed air installation may struggle to support increased production demand. Some common warning signs include:


• Pressure Instability: Air pressure drops when multiple machines operate simultaneously.

• Continuous Compressor Operation: Compressors run for longer periods or remain heavily loaded to meet increasing demand.

• Higher Energy Consumption: Additional operating hours and inefficient system conditions can increase electricity costs.

• Production Interruptions: Pneumatic machinery may experience insufficient air supply during peak demand.

• Increased Equipment Stress: Compressors and other system components may operate outside their intended operating conditions.

• Air Distribution Problems: Existing pipelines may create excessive pressure drops as more machines are connected.


These signs indicate that the compressed air system needs a proper performance assessment. However, the underlying cause should be identified before deciding whether additional compressor capacity is necessary.


Why Does Compressed Air Demand Increase During Industrial Expansion?


Production growth can change the compressed air requirements of a factory in several ways:


1. New Machinery Installation: Additional CNC machines, VMC machines, packaging equipment, pneumatic tools, and automated production lines increase total air consumption.

2. Simultaneous Machine Operation: More machines operating at the same time can increase peak airflow demand.

3. Longer Production Hours: Extended shifts and increased operating hours can change compressor loading patterns.

4. New Process Requirements: Additional manufacturing processes may require different airflow, working pressure, or compressed air quality.

5. Future Capacity Planning: Planned production expansion should be considered before upgrading the existing compressed air infrastructure.


Understanding these changes helps industries identify the right system configuration.


How Should an Industrial Compressed Air System Be Upgraded?


Upgrading a compressed air system is not simply about installing a higher HP compressor. The complete installation must be evaluated according to actual production requirements.


Important engineering considerations include:


✔ Actual Air Consumption: Measure or calculate the airflow requirements of existing and newly installed machinery.

✔ Peak and Average Demand: Analyze changing air consumption to determine suitable compressor capacity and control arrangements.

✔ Working Pressure: Check the pressure required at each application and account for losses across the system.

✔ Compressor Selection: Evaluate fixed-speed or VFD/VSD screw compressors and other suitable compressor technologies according to the demand profile.

✔ Air Treatment Capacity: Ensure dryers, filters, and moisture separators are appropriately sized for the required airflow and operating conditions.

✔ Receiver Tank Capacity: Review air storage requirements and compressor control strategy.

✔ Pipeline Infrastructure: Evaluate pipe diameter, layout, fittings, and pressure drops throughout the distribution network

✔ Future Expansion: Plan for expected production growth to avoid repeated system modifications.


A complete assessment helps determine whether the existing system needs additional capacity, equipment replacement, air distribution improvements, or a combination of upgrades.

Working Principle of a Reciprocating Piston Compressor


A reciprocating piston air compressor uses the movement of a piston inside a cylinder to compress air. During the intake stroke, air enters the cylinder through the inlet valve. During the compression stroke, the piston moves upward, reducing the available cylinder volume and increasing air pressure. The compressed air is then discharged through the outlet valve.


This compression mechanism is commonly used in industrial applications that require higher air pressures. The SJ 20 HP, 20 Bar configuration is intended for processes where conventional low-pressure compressed air systems may not meet the required operating pressure.
